name: Lymphatic pump

card.summary: An osteopathic manual technique that rhythmically compresses the chest or abdomen to encourage lymph flow, discussed for reducing swelling and puffiness.
card.note: Practised by osteopaths; not a cosmetic procedure with published appearance outcomes.

quick.overview:
The lymphatic pump is a hands-on osteopathic technique in which a practitioner applies rhythmic pressure to the chest wall or abdomen. It is intended to encourage the movement of lymph fluid through the body.

In appearance terms it is discussed in a chain: better lymph flow, less fluid retention, a less puffy look. Published human work has focused on medical outcomes such as immune markers and respiratory outcomes, not on cosmetic results.
quick.how: A trained osteopath performs the technique on a patient lying down, usually in a session of a few minutes combined with other manual work. People interested in facial or body puffiness sometimes add massage or compression by themselves.
quick.risks: Relative contraindications listed for the technique include fractures, abscesses or localized infection, and severe infection with fever above 39 C [1]. It is generally performed by licensed practitioners.

lead: The lymphatic pump technique is a manual osteopathic method described as intended to encourage lymph flow; the first modern version was developed in 1920, and osteopaths used lymphatic techniques in the late nineteenth century [1]. Practitioners apply rhythmic compressions, commonly to the thoracic region.

The lymphatic system moves fluid with a mix of passive forces and the intrinsic contractions of collecting vessels, a physiological pump studied in laboratory research [2][3]. Proponents of the technique reason that pressure changes from the manual pump add to this flow, and some people in the appearance space connect better fluid movement with reduced puffiness.
Human studies of the technique have examined blood cell counts, immune responses and post-operative lung outcomes rather than cosmetic outcomes [4][5][6].

chain: Manual pump applied to chest or abdomen
Less fluid pooling, potentially a less swollen look
angle.text: The link to appearance is through lymph drainage and reduced swelling. It is a claimed chain; published studies have measured other outcomes.

infobox: Fracture, abscess, severe infection with fever [1]

paras: Osteopathic lymphatic pump techniques include thoracic and pedal variants, described in a 2018 overview in the Journal of the American Osteopathic Association [4]. They sit within osteopathic manipulative medicine, founded by Andrew Taylor Still, who established the American School of Osteopathy in Kirksville, Missouri, in 1892 [1].

Reviews by osteopathic researchers describe the technique as enhancing lymphatic and immune function based on animal and human work [5]. Wikipedia's account of osteopathic manipulative medicine reports mixed reviews overall, calling parts of osteopathy pseudoscientific per several critics, while also noting moderate-quality evidence for low back pain [1].

A 1993 randomized trial of 42 cholecystectomy patients compared a thoracic lymphatic pump with incentive spirometry for preventing post-operative atelectasis [6]. A 2013 pilot randomized study examined blood cell counts after a lymphatic pump protocol in nursing home residents [7]. A 2014 randomized trial reported plasma cytokine release after osteopathic manipulation [8]. A 2019 review examined lymphatic pump manipulation in COPD [9]. No trial in these sources measured facial or cosmetic appearance.

timeline.event: First modern lymphatic pump version developed [1]
